#### 🇬🇧 London Heathrow (LHR) — 533 Delays, 64 Cancellations — Europe’s Worst Today

London Heathrow recorded the highest US-connected delays at 73, with live tracking reports showing average departure delays ranging between 39 and 48 minutes. Hub operators like British Airways initiate tactical cancellations to prevent aircraft and crew duty-time expirations from cascading into transatlantic schedules.

Heathrow’s 533 delays and 64 cancellations make it the single worst European airport today by both metrics. A 39% departure delay rate means more than one in three Heathrow departures ran late on Sunday — a significant operational failure at the world’s third-busiest international hub. [...] #### 🇦🇺 🇳🇿 Australian and New Zealand Travellers

Qantas operates the Kangaroo Route through Heathrow. Heathrow’s 39% delay rate on Sunday means Qantas services both arriving and departing London on October 4 were disrupted. Emirates (DXB hub), Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific all connect through European hubs affected today. If you were transiting Heathrow on a Qantas or oneworld partner itinerary on October 4, your Qantas Conditions of Carriage entitle you to rebooking at no additional cost.

### 🛡️ PART 6: EU261 and UK261 Rights — October 4, 2026 [...] Why Heathrow is most exposed: Heathrow operates at 98%+ slot utilisation — the closest to capacity of any major hub in Europe. When ATFM restrictions reduce the number of aircraft the network can process per hour, Heathrow has no slack in its schedule to absorb the difference. Every delayed aircraft blocks a gate needed for the next departure.

#### 🇫🇷 Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG) — 275 Delays, 33 Cancellations

Paris Charles de Gaulle recorded 275 delays and 33 cancellations, with a 23% departure delay rate and 17% arrival delay rate.

CDG’s 33 cancellations are the second-highest in Europe today. Air France, which operates CDG as its primary hub, accounts for the largest share of delays — alongside Lufthansa, which operates significant feeder connections between CDG and Frankfurt.

URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cjwgynnwyw2o
# Thunderstorms delay hundreds of Heathrow and Gatwick flights

Getty Images Easyjet planes on the tarmac at Gatwick airport.

Hundreds of flights at London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports have been delayed as the UK's air traffic control service warned disruption was expected to continue into Sunday.

More than 900 inbound and outbound flights at the two travel hubs have been delayed for up to 11 hours and dozens cancelled, according to tracker FlightAware, many due to thunderstorms.

NATS, the UK's air traffic control service, said adverse weather conditions meant aircraft needed to "avoid affected areas and be spaced further apart" and this would impact flights for the "remainder of Saturday and overnight". [...] However, other UK airports remain largely unaffected.

In an updated statement on Saturday afternoon, NATS said: "Severe thunderstorms across the south east of England and Europe continue to impact flights, and this is expected to continue for the remainder of today and overnight.

"To ensure the safety of the travelling public, aircraft need to avoid affected areas and be spaced further apart, which limits the number of flights that can operate safely.

"We understand disruption is frustrating, but we're working closely with airlines and airports to reduce disruption as much as possible.

"Passengers should continue to contact their airline for the latest information on their flight." [...] Gatwick and Heathrow advised passengers to check the status of their flights with airlines before travelling.

More than 474 flights arriving at or departing from Heathrow were delayed and another 439 in and out of Gatwick on Saturday, according to FlightAware.

Delays to affected flights vary. Heathrow's arrival board showed a British Airways flight from Santiago, Chile, that was due to land at 10:00 BST was not expected to arrive until 21:00.

## Thunderstorms delay hundreds of Heathrow and Gatwick flights

Europe-wide aviation agencyEurocontrol mapping showed the most severe air traffic control delays were in airspace between south-east England and north-western Europe, where the storm clouds were located.

However, other UK airports remain largely unaffected.
